Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Harjit Singh is a 64-year-old warehouse worker who came to treatment after months of sleeping only in fragments and feeling, as he put it, "finished." He is a married South Asian American man who had managed a steady, physically demanding routine for years, but since being held captive during a robbery at his warehouse, his days have become organized around getting through the evening and his nights around trying not to be overtaken by fear. The assault happened near the end of a late shift, when most of the loading bays were quiet and the light outside had already gone. Two men forced him into a back storage area, threatened him, and kept him shut in for hours. What stayed with him most vividly was the darkness, the sense of being trapped and unable to predict what would happen next, and the moment he noticed movement near some pallets and became convinced there were snakes in the room, whether real or imagined. He remembers staring into corners and at the floor, straining to see in the dim light, waiting for something else to strike.

In the weeks afterward, certain moments began to grip him with a force he did not expect. As the same time of day approached when the captivity had begun, he would become tense and restless at work, glancing at the clock and feeling his body brace. In the warehouse, where late afternoon shadows stretch between shelving and loading docks, talk from coworkers about pests or a photo of a snake on someone's phone could jolt him immediately back into that storage room. Night was worst. Waking in the dark or even anticipating bedtime made his chest tighten because darkness no longer felt neutral; it felt like the place where he had once been trapped and undefended. In those moments he responded by trying not to sleep at all, staying up in the living room with lights on until exhaustion forced him to lie down, asking his wife again and again to tell him he was safe and that nothing was wrong, and repeatedly checking his body for signs that something had happened to him without his noticing.

Those same triggers also keep him in a state of constant danger readiness. Near dusk he becomes intensely watchful, and once the sun goes down he says he cannot feel safe in the same way other people seem to. If he wakes in darkness, he sits upright listening, scanning the room, and when he walks through the parking lot after shift he repeatedly looks behind him to make sure no one is following. A passing mention of snakes or a picture of one is enough to make him sweep his eyes across the ground and corners automatically. His wife has noticed that even at home he checks locks, peers down the hallway, and startles if she enters a room unexpectedly, as though some part of him is still in that enclosed space waiting for the next threat.

Harjit has come to believe that what happened proved something terrible about him and the world. He is certain that he cannot stop bad things from happening to him; the captivity is no longer just a memory of being overpowered once, but evidence, to him, that safety can disappear without warning and that he will be helpless when it does. That belief sharpens his vigilance, especially at night. Because he sees danger as both unpredictable and unstoppable, he feels he has to stay superalert, to watch the dark, to check behind him, to remain on guard in ways that leave his body continually braced. He also avoids letting himself think directly about the event because he fears that if he really lets it into his mind, he will not be able to handle it.

Over time, the ways he has tried to manage have deepened these beliefs rather than easing them. The more he avoids sleep and lies awake with the lights on, the more the night itself comes to feel unlivable and overpowering, as if even bed is a place where he has no control. His repeated requests for reassurance bring only a few minutes of relief before the doubt returns, and each time it does he feels more defeated by how little comfort lasts. Checking his body again and again leaves him focused on vulnerability, searching for proof of harm and never feeling certain he is intact. He has begun to say, quietly, that he is not sure life is worth living anymore if this is what every evening will become.

Those habits have also made the triggers spread and harden. Because he delays sleep and remains awake into the darkest hours, he has more time to notice every creak, every shadow, every moment of waking in the night, so darkness itself has become increasingly charged. Because he keeps scanning his body and surroundings, he is quicker to notice sensations, sounds, and images that remind him of captivity. At work this has started to cost him. He lingers to avoid crossing the dim lot alone, loses focus near the end of shift when the light changes, and has become preoccupied whenever coworkers joke or talk about snakes. His wife, meanwhile, is exhausted by his nightly need for reassurance and frightened by how hopeless he sounds.

He finally sought help after a recent night when he woke in the dark, searched his body for injuries, checked the house repeatedly, and then sat awake until dawn convinced he would never feel safe again. What frightened him most was not just the fear itself, but the sense that his world had narrowed to avoiding night and enduring it. What he wants, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to come home from work, go to bed beside his wife, and believe that darkness is only darkness.
